cultural.vision_reason: A stone canopic jar with a falcon-head lid (Qebehsenuef), used in ancient Egyptian mummification rituals, made and used by ancient Egyptians. Clearly matches the claimed Egyptian ethnicity, though the museum labels it ceramic while it appears to be carved stone.

physical.title: Canopic Jar with Falcon's Head
physical.summary: In the process of mummification, the liver, lungs, stomach, and intestines were removed, separately embalmed, and stored in specialized jars known as canopic jars (after a sailor in Greek mythology, who died at the town of Canopus in the Nile Delta and was worshipped there in the form of a human-headed jar). Each organ was identified with one of four funerary deities collectively known as the Sons of Horus: the liver with Imsety (man's head), the lungs with Hapy (baboon's head), the stomach with Duamutef (jackal's head), and the intestines with Qebehsenuef (falcon's head). It was their duty to protect the deceased and restore to him his body parts in the hereafter.
